title: Are We Measuring the Wrong Things?
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Drawing on Kirabo Jackson's study of nearly half a million North Carolina students (as reported by Paul Tough), Stuart argues that schools may be measuring the wrong things. Jackson's proxy for noncognitive skills (attendance, suspensions, on-time progression and GPA) predicted college attendance, adult wages and avoiding arrest better than statewide standardized test scores. Stuart estimates the enormous educator time spent on state tests, then declines to condemn testing wholesale, praising the AP World History exam as a high-challenge, high-support assessment. His criticism is aimed at state tests that lack expert vetting, support materials, postsecondary recognition and any proven link to long-term outcomes. He closes with practical responses: support administrators, advocate for saner targets, keep doing the right classroom work, and talk with students about the noncognitive measures that matter.
points: Jackson's noncognitive proxy outpredicted state test scores for college attendance, wages and avoiding arrests.
Stuart estimates at least 35 million educator hours a year are aimed at state test results, a heavy cost if the tests measure the wrong thing.
He refuses to auto-disdain or auto-accept standardized tests, using the AP World History exam as a quality benchmark.
His practical advice is to support administrators, advocate for higher and saner targets, and do the right classroom work regardless of accountability pressure.
Teachers are urged to discuss attendance, discipline, credit and GPA with students because they matter for long-term outcomes.
quotes: It is entirely possible that your school or state or country is making dangerous assumptions about what should be measured (and therefore improved) and what shouldn't.
Jackson found that his noncognitive proxy measurement was a better predictor of select post-graduation outcomes than statewide standardized test results.

In reality, the average educator probably does spend at least ten hours per year laboring toward statewide standardized tests, which means, before we even calculate the hours spent creating these tests or the hours students spend taking them, we are looking at, at minimum, 35 million educator hours per year aimed at these results.
In short, the AP World History exam provides high challenge with high support. It's a good test.

And so even while I believe that we must not turn off our brains by auto-disdaining all standardized tests just because they are standardized tests, I also believe we must not turn off our brains by auto-accepting all standardized tests. They aren't all created equal — not even close.
Support my administrators, who face the brunt of the pressure to make state-wide standardized test scores improve. Don't conflate your administrator with your policymakers.
Even though we might be measuring the wrong things at a national or state-level, we still have agency.
